title: C# drill banks: csbootcamp and csdrills
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 bank-csharp row). Scope = csbootcamp modules 01-04 and csdrills modules 01-10. Sources and siblings are live drills of the modules that teach the idea. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Reconcile two collections by key with set operations (Except, Intersect, a dictionary join) instead of nested loops, and compare versions only for keys on both sides.
ideas.why: Nested loops are quadratic and easy to get wrong in both directions; reconciling by key makes 'added, removed, changed' three cheap, readable queries.
ideas.prompt: A client cache holds 20,000 items with id and version, and the server sends its current list. A colleague writes two nested foreach loops to find what to add, delete and refresh. What do you write instead?
ideas.answer: Index the server list by id in a dictionary. New items are server ids the cache does not have (Except), deleted ones are cache ids the server no longer has, and refreshed ones are ids on both sides whose versions differ. Each step is one pass, linear instead of 20,000 times 20,000 comparisons.

ideas.idea: Compose tasks on purpose: WhenAll for all results, WhenAny for the first, pass cancellation to the losers, and catch only the failures you expect.
ideas.why: Awaiting tasks one by one wastes time, unobserved losers keep running, and a catch-all hides the real fault behind a generic error.
ideas.prompt: A quote service asks three replicas for a price and uses the first answer, but the two slower calls keep running and their exceptions show up later as unobserved task errors. Fix the design.
ideas.answer: Start all three with a shared CancellationTokenSource, await Task.WhenAny for the first successful result, then cancel the token so the slower calls stop, and observe their tasks so failures are not lost. With WhenAll instead, inspect each task's exception rather than only the first one rethrown by await.

ideas.idea: Keep money in decimal or integer cents, never double, and name the rounding mode: .NET rounds midpoints to even by default, invoices usually round half away from zero.
ideas.why: Binary floating point cannot hold 0.10 exactly, and an unstated rounding mode makes totals disagree with the tax authority or the payment provider by a cent.
ideas.prompt: An invoice computes VAT with double and Math.Round, and some totals are a cent below what the accountant expects on amounts like 2.345. Explain both causes and the fix.
ideas.answer: double stores 2.345 as a nearby binary value, and Math.Round uses banker's rounding by default, so midpoints go to the even digit. Use decimal (or integer cents) and call Math.Round with MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero, or whatever rule the business states, at the step where it applies.

ideas.idea: Store and compare instants in UTC, convert to local time only at the edge, and remember that a local day can be 23 or 25 hours long.
ideas.why: Local timestamps in the database break sorting and math across zones, and adding 24 hours across a clock change lands an hour off.
ideas.prompt: A reminder 'every day at 09:00 local' is scheduled by adding 24 hours to the last run, stored as DateTime with Kind unspecified. After the spring clock change it fires at 10:00. What do you change?
ideas.answer: Store the moment as UTC and the rule as local wall-clock time plus a time zone. Compute each next run by taking tomorrow's date at 09:00 in that zone and converting it to UTC, instead of adding 24 hours. Keep DateTimeKind explicit when reading and writing the database.

ideas.idea: Use a [Flags] enum with powers of two for combinable rights, test with bit masks (any-of versus all-of), and parse untrusted values with a defined-value check.
ideas.why: HasFlag on a combined mask means all-of, which surprises people who wanted any-of, and Enum.TryParse accepts numbers that are not defined members.
ideas.prompt: A permission check `if (rights.HasFlag(Rights.Read | Rights.Write))` lets nobody in who has only Read, and a status parsed from a query string with TryParse accepts '99'. Explain both.
ideas.answer: HasFlag with a combined mask demands all the requested bits: all-of. For any-of test (rights & mask) != 0. TryParse succeeds for any number that fits the underlying type, defined or not, so check Enum.IsDefined (or a whitelist of names) before trusting the value.

ideas.idea: Derive identifiers and buckets from a stable hash (such as SHA-256) of a normalised, canonical input; string.GetHashCode changes between processes.
ideas.why: Hashing unnormalised text gives two ids for one user, and per-process hash codes put the same user in different buckets after every restart.
ideas.prompt: A feature-flag rollout puts users into buckets with `user.Email.GetHashCode() % 100`. After each deploy, users flip between the old and new UI, and 'Bob@x.com' and 'bob@x.com ' land in different buckets. Fix it.
ideas.answer: String hash codes in .NET are randomised per process, so the bucket changes on every restart. Normalise the input (trim, lower-case with invariant rules) and hash it with a stable algorithm such as SHA-256, then take the bucket from the hash bytes. The same user then always lands in the same bucket.

ideas.idea: Name the invariant first, then pick one tool for it: Interlocked for a single counter, lock for check-then-act, concurrent collections or channels for shared queues and maps.
ideas.why: Mixing tools or locking too little leaves races between the check and the act, and locking everything serialises the service.
ideas.prompt: A rate limiter checks `if (count < limit) count++;` from many threads, and a cache builds expensive entries twice under load. Which tool fits each, and why not the same one?
ideas.answer: The limiter's invariant spans a read and a write, so the check and the increment must happen together, inside one locked block or a compare-and-swap loop; Interlocked alone only makes the increment atomic. For the cache call GetOrAdd on a concurrent dictionary whose values are Lazy<T>, so each entry is built once even when callers race.

ideas.idea: Protect updates with ETags: the client sends If-Match with the version it read, the server answers 412 when it changed; If-None-Match: * makes create-only PUTs safe.
ideas.why: Without preconditions two clients editing the same record overwrite each other, and a retried create silently replaces data.
ideas.prompt: Two support agents open the same customer record, both edit it and save. The second save wipes the first agent's change without warning. Describe the HTTP-level fix.
ideas.answer: Return an ETag (a version or content hash) with every read. Require If-Match on PUT and PATCH, and compare it with the current version: if it differs, answer 412 Precondition Failed so the client reloads instead of overwriting. For create-only PUTs send If-None-Match: *, which fails when the resource already exists.
